Lubina Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Lubina, Slovakia

Not demolished. This cemetery once held about 40 graves; today, only two large black granite gravestones survive, bearing the names of the Deutsch and Plesz families, with the rest stolen by locals over the years. Jews first settled in Lubina in 1830, per the local property registry, but were expelled by locals at the end of WWI, accused of loyalty to the defeated Hungarian Kingdom and blamed for wartime price-gouging as shopkeepers; they relocated to nearby Nové Mesto nad Váhom, itself granted rights by King Béla IV in the 13th century and once the second-largest Jewish community in the former Kingdom of Hungary. During WWII, local villagers — including the Klimo family, later honored by Israel as Righteous Among the Nations and visited repeatedly by Israeli delegations led by descendants of Rabbi Dr. Aba-Armin Frieder — helped hide Jews. As part of the local Hurban partisan resistance group, two well-known Jews, Rudolf Vrba and Alfréd Israel Wetzler, fought against Nazi occupation; the pair had successfully escaped Auschwitz and authored the landmark 'Auschwitz Report,' the first detailed eyewitness account of the death camp's mass killings, which became known worldwide during the war. Commemorative stones honoring them were unveiled in the village in 2007.
